title: cip: dissect objects required for the Process Device Profiles
description:
The CIP Process Device Profiles added a series of CIP objects (Process Device Diagnostics Object, Process Measurement Value Object and Process Totalize Value Object). This MR extends the CIP dissector to support these 3 objects.

It also fixes the function `should_dissect_cip_response`. The current implementation instructs to continue parsing the frame when there is no data remaining but the status code is one of `CI_GRC_SUCCESS`, `CI_GRC_ATTR_LIST_ERROR`, `CI_GRC_SERVICE_ERROR` or `CI_GRC_INVALID_LIST_STATUS`. When no data remains, parsing should stop, regardless of the status code.

AI-Assisted: no

So does the comment now match the behavior or does the comment also need to be updated to reflect the updated behavior?
The comment now matches the intended behavior. The previous implementation was not correct.

This is definitely a worthwhile bugfix, but I'm not sure it's correct.
Is it desirable to have each element of the array as its own filterable item, or should this just be an array of data (i.e. keep total_len and get rid of the for loop)

Well, both ways are correct. Since there was a for loop containing a `proto_tree_add_item` I assumed that the author of the original code wanted to have individual elements. That's also what's done in the case `cip_uint_array` a couple lines below. 
I personally don't care, but my intent was not to change the existing behavior.
@mmann78 just tell me if you want me to use a single element for the whole array. But in that case, we should also update the case `cip_uint_array` to be consistent.

After thinking a bit about this, I believe it's better to keep individual elements. You can have arrays of anything in CIP. In the case of `cip_uint_array`, so an array of 16-bit integers (little-endian), as a user, I would expect the dissector to present me an array of usable values and not just one large byte array, where I would have to do split values and do the little-endian gymnastics to understand the values.
If that's the better way to handle an array of 16-bit integers, or an array of structs, then why should we treat an array of 8-bit values differently?
Can we please not mix ptvcursor APIs with a dissector that doesn't already have them?  I think consistency in the code of the dissector is more important.
Sure, I understand your point. ptvcursor just make the code much more easier to read and to understand than having to deal with offsets, parsed lengths, etc. I'll change it.

Done, I've removed the ptvcursor API and switched back the to "classic" API. May I suggest adding this "rule" about not mixing ptvcursor with the classic API to the developer documentation though?
I understand the consistency rationale, but at the same time, the ptvcursor is much less error-prone. It's very easy to forget incrementing an offset, or passing the wrong offset to a `proto_tree_add_item()`. ptvcursor makes it so much easier and from a software design point of view, this helps keeping the "single level of abstraction" principle. Dealing with "high-level" protocol fields and with "low-level" pointers and buffer offsets at the same time makes the code much less readable.
Is there any plan to encourage the usage of ptvcursor?
